report: Field crew overrode the pressure relief valve trip on a separator to keep production running through a shift change. No release occurred.
reason: Removing overpressure protection risks vessel rupture regardless of whether an event occurred this time.

report: Operator taped over the low-oil-pressure shutdown sensor on a standby generator because of nuisance trips; engine ran normally the rest of the shift.
reason: Disabling an engine protection interlock removes the barrier against catastrophic mechanical failure and fire.

report: Technician found a jammed emergency-stop button on the conveyor, reported it at once, and locked the line out instead of continuing to run it.
reason: Correct reporting and lockout response meant no bypass occurred and no exposure resulted.

report: Contractor briefly jumpered the door interlock on a low-voltage control cabinet to reset a tripped breaker; received a mild static shock.
reason: Voltage and stored energy involved were too low to cause serious harm even with the interlock defeated.

report: H2S alarm at the wellhead was silenced by the crew due to repeated false alarms during a routine check. No gas release occurred that shift.
reason: Silencing a toxic-gas alarm removes the only warning barrier against a potentially fatal exposure.

report: Used a screwdriver to hold down the guard interlock on an angle grinder to finish a rush job. Grinder kicked back and tore the glove; hand uninjured.
reason: Defeating a rotating-equipment guard exposes the operator to severe laceration or worse; the kickback shows the barrier failure was real.

report: Housekeeping propped open a fire door fitted with an alarm sensor to move furniture through. No fire event occurred.
reason: The specific control bypassed posed no immediate energy-release risk to personnel present.

report: Rig crew defeated the driller's console interlock that blocks pipe rotation during connections, to save time. Connection completed without incident.
rules: Bypassing Safety Controls; Line of Fire
reason: Defeating this interlock exposes crew in the red zone to being caught in rotating pipe, a known fatality mechanism, whether or not this attempt caused harm.

report: New hire was seen wiring down a pressure relief valve lever during a hydrotest; senior operator stopped him before pressure was applied.
reason: Intent and setup to defeat overpressure protection is a high-fatal-potential precursor even though it was caught before pressure was applied.

report: Crew removed a machine guard to clean out jammed material, guard was reinstalled correctly before restarting; no exposure occurred.
reason: Guard was removed only while the machine was fully isolated and restored before operation resumed.

report: Worker entered a nitrogen-purged tank to retrieve a dropped tool without a permit or atmosphere test. Exited within seconds, unharmed.
reason: Entering an oxygen-deficient space without testing can cause fatal asphyxiation within seconds; no injury this time does not reduce the hazard present.

report: Confined space entry team completed full gas testing, permit, and attendant briefing before entering a vessel for inspection. Work completed normally.
reason: All required barriers were in place and functioning; no unmanaged hazard was present.

report: Employee climbed partway into a sewage pit to clear a blockage using a rope tied around his waist, no supplied-air or gas monitor used. No symptoms reported.
reason: Toxic and oxygen-deficient atmospheres in sewage pits are a classic fatality scenario; absence of symptoms does not indicate absence of risk.

report: Vessel entry was cancelled after gas testing showed elevated H2S; job was rescheduled with forced ventilation and re-tested before proceeding.
reason: The hazard was identified and controlled before entry, preventing exposure.

report: A rigger stuck his head into an open manhole to check for a dropped wrench without testing the atmosphere, then withdrew immediately.
reason: Even brief exposure to an untested confined-space atmosphere can be fatal if toxic or oxygen-deficient gas is present.

report: Contractor entered a tank previously used for diesel storage, atmosphere tested clear, full PPE and standby attendant present throughout the job.
reason: Full controls were verified and in place; risk was actively managed to a low level.

report: Employee received a scraped elbow climbing out of a properly permitted, gas-free storage vessel after completing routine inspection.
reason: An injury occurred, but the confined-space entry itself followed proper controls; the scrape was unrelated to atmospheric or engulfment hazards.

report: Two workers propped open the confined-space entry hatch and skipped the atmosphere retest after a 45-minute break, then re-entered.
reason: Atmosphere can change quickly once a space is re-sealed or disturbed; skipping the retest removes a critical safeguard against toxic buildup.

report: Standby attendant left post to answer a phone call while a colleague remained inside a confined space for approximately two minutes.
reason: Loss of the attendant removes the only means of rescue or alarm if the entrant is incapacitated by the atmosphere inside.

report: Worker used a full-body harness and retrieval line while entering a small-diameter pipe run for internal inspection, per permit requirements.
reason: Rescue and retrieval provisions were in place as required, reducing fatal potential even in a restrictive space.

report: Driver was texting while travelling at highway speed on the site access road; vehicle drifted onto the shoulder before being corrected.
reason: Distracted driving at speed with a lane-departure event carries high potential for a fatal collision or rollover.

report: Field supervisor completed a 40 km night drive to site after logging 14 hours awake, arrived without incident.
reason: Extended fatigue significantly raises the likelihood of a severe crash; arriving safely does not indicate the risk was low.

report: Driver stopped at a rest area after feeling drowsy during a long haul, napped 20 minutes, then continued the trip.
reason: Fatigue was recognized and proactively managed before it became a hazard.

report: Light vehicle was found with a bald rear tyre after a routine yard inspection; no trip had yet been taken with the vehicle in that condition.
reason: A tyre blowout at speed is a known cause of fatal rollovers; the defect being caught before use does not remove the precursor risk it represents.

report: Driver failed to wear a seatbelt on a short 200-metre move within a fenced yard at walking pace.
reason: Extremely low speed and short distance mean the kinetic energy involved was minimal despite the seatbelt violation.

report: Truck carrying drill pipe was driven through a flooded low-water crossing against site advisories; vehicle made it across without incident.
reason: Vehicles can be swept away or stall in floodwater, a known cause of drowning fatalities, regardless of this crossing's outcome.

report: Vehicle involved in a minor parking-lot scrape with a bollard while reversing at low speed; only cosmetic damage to the bumper.
reason: Low speed and stationary object involved meant negligible risk of serious injury.

report: Employee drove a company vehicle after taking a sedating antihistamine, reported it and swapped with a colleague before departure.
reason: The hazard was identified and mitigated before the vehicle was operated.

report: Convoy of two site vehicles was found tailgating each other at close distance on a gravel road in poor visibility due to dust.
reason: Close following distance in low visibility on unsealed roads is a well-documented precursor to fatal multi-vehicle collisions.

report: Driver exceeded the posted site speed limit by 10 km/h briefly while overtaking a slow-moving grader on a straight, clear section of road.
reason: Modest overspeed on a clear straight section with good visibility carried limited additional risk.

report: Maintenance technician began disassembling a pump for repair without applying lockout/tagout; pump was later confirmed to be electrically isolated by chance.
reason: Working on equipment without verifying isolation is fatal-potential regardless of whether the equipment happened to be de-energized.

report: Crew completed full lockout/tagout with individual locks and a zero-energy verification test before opening a hydraulic line for repair.
reason: All required isolation steps were performed and verified, controlling the hazard effectively.

report: A technician removed his own lock from a shared lockout point before confirming with the rest of the crew that all work was complete.
reason: Premature lock removal can re-energize equipment while other workers are still exposed, a common precursor to fatal energization incidents.

report: Operator briefly touched a de-energized breaker panel to confirm it felt cool before starting work, in addition to following full LOTO procedure.
reason: Proper isolation and verification were already completed; the additional check added no meaningful risk.

report: Employee attempted to clear a jam inside a running conveyor belt by reaching in with a stick instead of stopping and isolating the equipment.
reason: Reaching into operating machinery risks entanglement and traumatic amputation, a classic energy-isolation fatality mechanism.

report: Electrician found a lockout tag left on a panel from a completed job two days earlier and removed it after confirming with the supervisor.
reason: Proper verification was performed before removing the tag; no unmanaged hazard existed.

report: Two contractors worked on opposite ends of the same hydraulic system, each assuming the other had verified isolation; neither had.
reason: Unverified assumptions about isolation status between multiple parties working the same system is a significant precursor to unexpected energy release.

report: Worker received a minor pinch to a finger while manually rotating an isolated, de-energized valve wheel during scheduled maintenance.
reason: Equipment was correctly isolated; the injury was a mechanical pinch unrelated to stored or residual energy.

report: Technician skipped the zero-energy verification step after applying LOTO, relying on the tag alone before opening the equipment housing.
reason: Skipping verification means residual or incorrectly isolated energy sources could remain live, undermining the entire control.

report: Job required isolation of both electrical and pneumatic energy; crew isolated electrical only and began work, unaware of the stored air pressure.
reason: Incomplete isolation leaving a secondary energy source live is a frequent cause of fatal releases during maintenance.

report: Welder began cutting a pipe section without a hot work permit or fire watch present; no fire resulted.
reason: Unpermitted hot work near flammable materials carries high fatal and fire potential independent of this specific outcome.

report: Hot work permit was issued, area cleared of combustibles, fire extinguisher and fire watch posted before welding began on a structural beam.
reason: All required controls were verified in place before work started.

report: Grinding sparks from routine metal fabrication ignited nearby oily rags that had not been cleared from the work area; fire was extinguished quickly with no injuries.
reason: Actual ignition of combustible material near hot work confirms the fatal-potential pathway was real, even though it was contained.

report: Contractor performed hot work on a tank that had previously held flammable product without confirming it was gas-freed and certified safe.
reason: Welding on an unconfirmed vessel risks explosion from residual flammable vapors, a known cause of multiple fatalities in industry.

report: Cutting torch flashback arrestor was checked and confirmed functional as part of pre-job equipment inspection before hot work began.
reason: Equipment safeguards were verified functional before use, reducing potential for flashback fire.

report: Worker sustained a minor burn to a finger from a hot weld bead while wearing all required PPE and following permit conditions correctly.
reason: An injury occurred, but it was a localized contact burn unrelated to fire or explosion potential, and all major controls were followed.

report: Fire watch left the hot work area five minutes early, before the standard cooldown period had elapsed, to attend another task.
reason: Smoldering material can ignite after work stops; leaving before the cooldown period removes the barrier meant to catch delayed ignition.

report: Hot work was conducted directly above an open drain connected to the process sewer without a drain cover, though no incident occurred.
reason: Sparks entering process drains can ignite flammable vapors accumulated in the sewer system, a documented cause of major incidents.

report: Team relocated a hot work job by ten metres after identifying nearby flammable vapor sources during the pre-job risk assessment.
reason: The hazard was proactively identified and eliminated before work began.

report: Welding curtain was not deployed during hot work near a walkway, though no bystanders passed through during the job.
reason: Absence of the curtain created ongoing exposure potential to arc flash or spark for anyone who might have walked past.

report: Worker walked directly beneath a suspended load being repositioned by a crane to retrieve a dropped tool. No load drop occurred.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Being under a suspended load is a top cause of struck-by fatalities regardless of whether the load was dropped this time.

report: Exclusion zone was established and enforced around a suspended load throughout a crane lift; no personnel entered the zone.
reason: The line-of-fire hazard was actively controlled by maintaining the exclusion zone.

report: Employee stood beside an operating pipe wrench under tension while a colleague applied force, in the direct path if the wrench slipped.
reason: Stored energy in a wrench under load can release suddenly and strike anyone standing in its path, a recognized fatality mechanism.

report: A wrench slipped from a technician's grip and fell into a barricaded, unoccupied area below.
reason: The exclusion zone below the work platform was respected and no person was exposed to the falling object.

report: Two employees worked on opposite sides of a wall being demolished with a hydraulic breaker, unable to see or communicate with each other.
reason: Debris or wall sections could strike the unseen worker on the opposite side without warning.

report: Worker received a bruise to the shin after being brushed by a slow-moving golf cart in a walkway at very low speed.
reason: Low speed and minor contact meant limited transferred energy despite the line-of-fire exposure.

report: Employee positioned himself between a reversing forklift and a fixed wall to guide the operator, with no spotter or horn signal used.
reason: Being pinned between a moving vehicle and a fixed structure is a well-known crushing fatality scenario.

report: Reversing alarm and spotter were both used correctly while a forklift backed into a tight loading area with pedestrians nearby.
reason: Standard controls for vehicle line-of-fire hazards were followed correctly.

report: A tensioned wire rope snapped during a rigging job and struck a support structure two metres from where a worker had been standing moments earlier.
reason: A whipping wire rope under tension can cause fatal or severe injury on release; the near-miss proximity confirms real exposure existed.

report: Crew waited behind the marked barrier line while a jackhammer operator worked on a section of concrete slab ahead of them.
reason: Maintaining distance behind the barrier controlled the exposure to flying debris.

report: Crane operator lifted a load exceeding the rated capacity for the current boom angle; the lift was completed without the load dropping.
reason: Exceeding rated lift capacity risks sudden structural failure of the crane or rigging, a major cause of fatal lifting incidents.

report: Lift plan was reviewed, rigging inspected, and load weight confirmed against crane charts before a routine equipment lift.
reason: All standard lift-planning controls were completed correctly before the lift proceeded.

report: Rigger used a sling with visible fraying to lift a moderately heavy steel beam; sling held for the duration of the lift.
reason: A visibly damaged sling can fail without warning during a lift, risking a dropped load onto personnel below.

report: A tag line was used to control load rotation during a crane lift over an active work area, keeping the load steady throughout.
reason: Proper control measures reduced the risk of uncontrolled load movement.

report: Two lifting points were used instead of the four specified in the rigging plan for an irregularly shaped load, lift proceeded without incident.
reason: Under-rigging an irregular load increases the chance of the load shifting or falling during the lift.

report: Worker's hand was pinched between a pallet and a forklift fork while guiding a low, slow-speed lift in a warehouse aisle.
reason: Low lift height and slow speed limited the potential severity despite the injury that occurred.

report: Crane was operated near an overhead power line without the required minimum clearance distance being confirmed beforehand.
reason: Contact between crane components and live power lines is a well-documented cause of multiple fatalities.

report: Load chart and outrigger positioning were verified by a certified rigger before a crane lift near the edge of a slope.
reason: Certified verification of ground and rigging conditions controlled the primary tip-over hazard.

report: Personnel remained under a raised forklift load while adjusting a strap, rather than lowering the load first.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Working beneath a suspended or raised load is a recurring precursor to fatal crush injuries.

report: Lifting bag used to raise a section of pipe was rated well above the actual load weight, with a documented safety margin applied.
reason: Conservative capacity margin reduced the likelihood of equipment failure during the lift.

report: Contractor began excavation work near a marked underground pipeline corridor without obtaining a permit or verifying utility locations.
reason: Unauthorized excavation near buried pipelines risks rupture of high-pressure or flammable lines, a known cause of fatal incidents.

report: Permit to work was completed, reviewed by the area authority, and briefed to the full crew before maintenance began on a live process unit.
reason: Proper authorization and communication controls were in place before work started.

report: Night shift crew continued a job past the permit's expiry time without renewing it, conditions in the area had not changed.
reason: Working outside a valid permit period removes the formal check that conditions remain safe to continue.

report: Job was paused and the permit was formally re-validated after a shift handover introduced a new work crew to the site.
reason: The re-validation step ensured the new crew was briefed and conditions were reconfirmed safe.

report: Worker began isolating a valve on a live line based on a verbal instruction from a colleague, without a written permit or isolation certificate.
reason: Verbal-only authorization on a live system removes formal checks designed to prevent working on the wrong or unisolated equipment.

report: Simultaneous operations form was completed and reviewed before scaffolding work began near an active crane lift zone.
reason: Coordination between the two activities was formally reviewed and managed before work began.

report: Employee received a minor cut while filling out permit-required paperwork on a clipboard with a sharp edge before starting an authorized job.
reason: The injury was unrelated to the job hazard itself and occurred during an otherwise correctly authorized process.

report: Two separate crews were both issued permits for overlapping work on the same pipe section without either being made aware of the other.
reason: Uncoordinated simultaneous work on the same equipment can result in one crew being exposed to hazards created by the other.

report: Permit was issued for hot work but did not specify that a nearby vent was still connected to the process, work proceeded on this basis.
reason: An incomplete permit hazard assessment left a live connection unaccounted for, risking ignition of process vapors.

report: Supervisor conducted a pre-job toolbox talk covering permit conditions and site-specific hazards before releasing the crew to start work.
reason: Clear communication of authorized scope and hazards reduced the chance of unauthorized or unsafe deviations.

report: Worker leaned out from a scaffold platform without a harness to reach a fitting slightly out of arm's reach; did not fall.
reason: Leaning beyond a guarded platform edge without fall protection carries high fatal potential regardless of this outcome.

report: Full-body harness was worn and correctly anchored to an approved point before work began on an elevated platform above six metres.
reason: Fall protection was correctly used, controlling the primary hazard of working at height.

report: Employee used a stepladder on uneven ground without securing it, ladder wobbled but the worker regained balance and did not fall.
reason: An unsecured ladder on uneven ground is a well-known precursor to falls from height, regardless of whether this attempt ended safely.

report: Scaffold was inspected and tagged by a competent person before use, with guardrails and toe boards confirmed in place.
reason: Standard scaffold inspection and guarding controls were verified before workers accessed the structure.

report: Worker climbed onto an elevated pipe rack without a harness to inspect a fitting, standing approximately four metres above ground level.
reason: Unprotected access to an elevated structure at this height carries a high risk of fatal fall.

report: Employee received a minor scrape to the forearm while descending a properly secured and inspected ladder, following all access procedures correctly.
reason: An injury occurred, but proper fall-protection procedures were followed and the height/energy involved was low.

report: Roof access hatch was left open and unguarded near a walking path for several hours during a maintenance job, no one approached the opening.
reason: An open, unguarded fall hazard on a walked route creates ongoing potential for a fatal fall regardless of whether anyone approached it during this period.

report: Guardrails were temporarily removed to move materials onto a platform, and were reinstalled immediately before any personnel accessed the area again.
reason: The fall hazard was controlled by sequencing the work so no personnel were exposed while guarding was down.

report: Two workers stood on the top rung of a stepladder, above the manufacturer's rated standing line, to reach an overhead cable tray.
reason: Standing above the rated line significantly increases the chance of losing balance and falling from an unstable position.

report: Fall arrest system was inspected before the shift and a worker's harness was found to have a damaged D-ring; harness was replaced before work began.
reason: The defect was identified and corrected before any exposure to a fall occurred.

report: A crane operator swung a loaded pallet directly over two technicians working on the ground below.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Positioning a suspended load directly above personnel exposes them to a potentially fatal strike if the load or rigging fails.

report: Employee stood beneath an overhead crane hook while it repositioned a large steel beam across the yard.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Standing under a moving overhead load is a direct exposure to a heavy falling-object hazard.

report: Rigger walked underneath a raised excavator bucket to reach tools on the far side of the site.
reason: Passing beneath a raised, heavy piece of equipment exposes the worker to being crushed if it drops or swings unexpectedly.

report: A technician reached up to adjust a sling while a suspended engine block hung directly above his head.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Working directly beneath a suspended heavy object puts the worker in the direct path of a fatal strike if the load shifts.

report: Two workers paused for a break in the shade cast by a crane's suspended concrete slab overhead.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Remaining under a suspended load for any reason, including incidentally, carries the same fatal strike potential as working there.

report: A forklift carried a raised pallet of pipe fittings across a walkway while a pedestrian passed directly beneath the forks.
reason: A raised load passing over a pedestrian is a direct line-of-fire exposure to a falling-object strike.

report: Maintenance crew stood under a gantry crane's load path to guide a hanging valve assembly into position by hand.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Manually guiding a load from directly beneath it removes any margin of safety if the load drops.

report: A worker crossed under an active tower crane's boom line to shortcut to the site office, without checking for an ongoing lift.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Crossing beneath an active crane's load path exposes a person to being struck without warning by a load or falling rigging.

report: The crane's exclusion zone was clearly marked and no personnel entered the area beneath the suspended load during the entire lift.
reason: Maintaining the exclusion zone meant no one was ever exposed to the suspended load overhead.

report: Load was lifted only after all personnel moved outside the marked barrier line surrounding the lift area.
rules: Line of Fire; Safe Mechanical Lifting
reason: Personnel were cleared from the hazard zone before the lift began, removing any exposure to the suspended load.

report: A pallet was lifted two feet off the ground to check the forklift's hydraulics, with no one within ten metres of the load.
reason: Minimal lift height and complete absence of nearby personnel meant no meaningful exposure existed.

report: Driver scraped a traffic cone while parking at speed.
reason: Low speed maneuver.

report: Vehicle involved in a parking-lot scrape with a bollard while reversing at parking speed.
reason: Stationary object involved meant low risk of serious injury.

report: Employee stepped on the first rung of a ladder without tying off but stepped down immediately.
reason: Very low height and minimal fall risk.

report: Full-body harness was worn and correctly anchored before work began on an elevated platform.
reason: Fall protection was used and controlled the hazard.
